covers.quote: Use initial capitals for the titles of individual academics and professionals
Use lower case if you use a title generically.

examples.note: Honorary academic title with initial capitals

parts.quote: Adjunct Professor Monty Chiratte

examples.note: Generic use in lower case

parts.quote: All general surgeons at the hospital attended Wednesday’s forum.

rules.quote: The academic and professional titles held by individuals usually have initial capitals.
rules.violation_condition: an individual's academic or professional title written in lower case when naming or addressing them
when: applies to honorary titles
does not apply when using a title generically
rules.why: G-1 and G-4: heading consolidated with body rule and generic exception recorded under when.

covers.quote: Use full titles in certain contexts
to introduce an individual as speaker
in address and signature blocks in correspondence
in official records of proceedings
in lists in organisational publications such as annual reports
if it is important to know where an individual works.

examples.note: Full title in presentation context

parts.quote: Professor Margaret Sheil AO, Vice-Chancellor and President, Queensland University of Technology

rules.specification: A full title includes the title or honorific (with initial capitals), name, post-nominals, position and organisation.
rules.violation_condition: failing to use a full title (including title/honorific, name, post-nominals, position, and organisation) in display contexts, speaker introductions, official proceedings, correspondence address/signature blocks, or formal organisational lists
when: when introducing an individual as speaker
in address and signature blocks in correspondence
in official records of proceedings
in lists in organisational publications such as annual reports
if it is important to know where an individual works
rules.why: G-1 and G-2: heading and list items consolidated into one rule on full title contexts.

covers.quote: Also use initial capitals for the shortened forms of titles.

examples.note: Title before name capitalised ('Professor Rufus Black'), generic title before that in lower case ('vice-chancellor and president')

parts.quote: Our new vice-chancellor and president is Professor Rufus Black.

examples.note: Shortened form 'Dr' capitalised immediately before name

parts.quote: We welcome Dr Jamilah Mulyadi to our clinic. Dr Mulyadi is now available for skin examinations.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for titles that appear immediately before a person’s name.
rules.violation_condition: a title immediately preceding a person's name written in lower case, unless the title is generic
when: unless the title is generic (for example, preceded by 'the' or a modifier like 'former')
also applies to shortened forms of titles
rules.why: G-2: shortened form capitalisation is part of the same condition as full titles before a name.

covers.quote: Never use the shortened form of the title in body text (‘Prof’ for example), except for the contraction ‘Dr’.
‘Dr’ is an exception in all instances.

examples.note: Spelt-out titles preferred in image caption

parts.quote: Left to right: Associate Professor Sara Baird, Vice-Chancellor Tom Dhillon, Dean Frank Ealing, Adjunct Professor Olena Iraklidis, Dr Celia Nieminen

examples.note: Shortened forms permitted only for limited space

parts.quote: Left to right: Assoc Prof S Baird, VC T Dhillon, Dean F Ealing, Adj Prof O Iraklidis, Dr C Nieminen

examples.note: Spelt out in body text

parts.quote: This year’s graduate cohort asked Deputy Vice-Chancellor Jonquil Johansson to moderate their debate.

examples.note: Shortened form used in body text

parts.quote: DVC Jonquil Johansson to moderate their debate.

rules.quote: Only use shortened forms of titles in limited circumstances.
rules.specification: Write titles in full in body text. Shortened forms may only be used when space is limited (e.g. tables, constrained captions), except 'Dr' which is always permitted.
rules.violation_condition: using a shortened form or abbreviation of a title (such as 'Prof' or 'PVC') in running text where space is not constrained, other than 'Dr'
when: 'Dr' is an exception and may be used in all instances
shortened forms may be used in tables or where space is limited, provided full forms are listed in a note or body text
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidates restriction on shortened forms across the page.

covers.quote: when you address someone directly
for salutations in correspondence.

examples.note: Official title replacing a specific name

parts.quote: The Vice-Chancellor of the University of Tasmania visited last week.

examples.note: Salutation

parts.quote: Dear Chancellor

examples.note: Direct address

parts.quote: ‘We note your concerns Doctor. Thank you for bringing this evidence before the committee’.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for official titles that replace a name.
rules.violation_condition: an official title replacing a specific person's name (e.g. direct address, salutation, or specific office) written in lower case
when: when addressing someone directly
for salutations in correspondence
when the official full title stands in for a specific named individual (e.g. 'The Vice-Chancellor of the University of Tasmania')
rules.why: G-1 and G-2: combines specific cases of titles replacing a name.

covers.quote: These other uses include abbreviated titles and titles given by an organisation to a role or position. Academic and professional organisations might capitalise such titles as a mark of respect or status, but this is not Australian Government style. Treat them as generic and use lower case.

examples.note: Abbreviated title replacing name in lower case

parts.quote: The vice-chancellor visited Burnie campus last week.

rules.quote: For all other uses, titles that replace a name should be lower case.
rules.specification: Applies to abbreviated titles and generic role titles replacing a name (e.g. 'the vice-chancellor visited Burnie campus').
rules.violation_condition: an abbreviated title or generic role/position title replacing a name written with initial capitals
rules.why: G-4: rule covering lower-casing other titles replacing names.

covers.quote: There is one exception. Only use initial capitals for titles after a name in a full title.

examples.note: Descriptive title after name in lower case in body text

parts.quote: They met with Associate Professor Dianne Stephens OAM, medical director of the National Critical Care and Trauma Response Centre.

examples.note: Full title context with initial capitals after name

parts.quote: Associate Professor Dianne Stephens OAM, Medical Director, National Critical Care and Trauma Response Centre

rules.quote: Use lower case for most titles that appear after a name.
rules.violation_condition: a descriptive or generic title appearing after a person's name written with initial capitals outside of a full title context
when: exception: use initial capitals for titles after a name in a full title (such as in address/signature blocks, official lists, or speaker introductions)
rules.why: G-2: rule for titles following a name and its full-title exception.

covers.quote: titles that describe a named individual
plural titles
common nouns.

examples.note: Descriptive title after name in lower case

parts.quote: Professor Bartlett, the university’s vice-chancellor, welcomed alumni to the reception.

examples.note: Title before name modified by 'the' in lower case

parts.quote: The research fellow Lydia Mbegngue wrote extensively on this topic.

examples.note: Plural title in lower case

parts.quote: Several postdoctoral fellows in the research facility met last week.

examples.note: Common noun in lower case

parts.quote: A provost oversees a university’s academic performance.

examples.note: Title before name modified by 'former' in lower case

parts.quote: They met with former medical director Tom Perera.

rules.quote: Use lower case for titles used in a generic way
rules.specification: Generic titles include plural titles, common nouns, descriptive titles following a name, or titles before a name preceded by 'the' or modifiers like 'former'.
rules.violation_condition: capitalising a generic title, such as a plural title, common noun, title describing an individual, or title modified by 'the' or an adjective
rules.why: G-1 and G-2: heading and definition of generic titles consolidated.

covers.quote: Use title, name and post-nominals at first mention
If you mention the individual again, only use the title and last name. Some academic titles have an accepted abbreviated title you can use after the first mention.

examples.note: First mention with title and full name; subsequent mention with abbreviated title and surname

parts.quote: Emeritus Professor Stephen Duckett has extensive experience in health care at senior leadership level. Professor Duckett’s membership of the RMIT Council concludes in 2022.

rules.quote: The first time you mention someone in body text, use their academic or professional title before their first name and last name, followed by post-nominals.
rules.violation_condition: mentioning an academic or professional in body text for the first time without their title before their first and last name, or failing to switch to title and last name only on subsequent mentions
when: on subsequent mentions, only use the title and last name (or accepted abbreviated title and last name)
rules.why: G-1 and G-2: first mention format and subsequent mention format are two sides of the mention rule.

covers.quote: Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles

examples.note: No commas between post-nominals

parts.quote: Professor Sally Wheeler OBE MRIA FAcSS FAAL

rules.quote: Don’t use commas before or between post-nominals.
rules.violation_condition: a comma placed immediately before or between post-nominals
rules.why: G-4: explicit negative constraint on punctuation around post-nominals.

covers.quote: Use post-nominals at first mention only
The first time you write a name in body text, use the academic and professional title along with the first and last name. Include the post-nominal for a civil or military honour in the title.

examples.note: First mention has post-nominal AO; second mention omits it

parts.quote: Dr Ziggy Switkowski AO has been chancellor of RMIT since 2011. Dr Switkowski is also chair of NBN Co.

rules.quote: If you mention the name again, use the title and last name, but don’t include the post-nominal.
rules.violation_condition: including a post-nominal when naming an individual on a second or subsequent mention in body text
when: applies in body text
rules.why: G-4: specific rule requiring omission of post-nominals on repeat mention.

covers.quote: Include post-nominals in the shortened forms of titles

examples.note: Post-nominals retained with shortened title and initials

parts.quote: Attendees: Dr Z Switkowski AO, Prof M Bean CBE, Dr S Andrews, Ms J Latchford, Prof S Duckett, Ms T McLaughin and Mr D Hoogstra.

rules.quote: Retain any post-nominals for civil and military honours when using the shortened forms of titles.
rules.violation_condition: omitting civil and military honours post-nominals when using shortened forms of titles
rules.why: G-4: heading restated by single sentence rule.

examples.note: Either Dr or PhD, never both together

parts.quote: Dr Zdenka Svoboda or Zdenka Svoboda PhD

rules.quote: Don’t include both ‘Dr’ (doctorate) and ‘PhD’ (Doctor of Philosophy) for the one name.
rules.specification: Use either the title 'Dr' or the post-nominal 'PhD' / 'LLD', but not both.
rules.violation_condition: using both 'Dr' and 'PhD' (or a PhD equivalent like 'LLD') for the same person's name
when: does not apply to medical practitioners who hold a doctorate (e.g. 'Dr ... MD PhD')
rules.why: G-4: distinct negative constraint on combining Dr and PhD.

rules.quote: Don’t include post-nominals for master and bachelor degrees in correspondence.
rules.violation_condition: including bachelor or master degree post-nominals in correspondence
when: applies in correspondence (emails and letters)
rules.why: G-4: explicit negative constraint on degree post-nominals in correspondence.

examples.note: Dame after Chancellor

parts.quote: Chancellor Dame Leonie Kramer AC DBE

examples.note: Sir after Chancellor

parts.quote: Chancellor Sir Albert Axon KBE

rules.quote: Use ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’ after the academic title.
rules.specification: For an academic who is knighted, place 'Sir' or 'Dame' directly after the academic title.
rules.violation_condition: placing 'Sir' or 'Dame' before an academic title (e.g. Sir Professor instead of Professor Sir)
when: applies when an academic has been knighted
rules.why: G-4: specific order rule for academic titles combined with knighthoods.

covers.quote: Don’t include a comma after these phrases.

examples.note: No commas after opening or closing

parts.quote: Dear Associate Professor … Yours faithfully

examples.note: Incorrect commas after salutation and valediction

parts.quote: Dear Associate Professor, … Yours faithfully,

rules.quote: Don’t include a comma after these phrases.
rules.specification: Australian Government style writes salutations and valedictions without trailing commas.
rules.violation_condition: a comma placed after a correspondence salutation or valediction (e.g. 'Dear Chancellor,', 'Yours sincerely,')
when: applies to opening salutations and closing valedictions in correspondence
rules.why: G-4: unified punctuation prohibition for correspondence salutations/valedictions across sections.

rules.quote: For Australian correspondence, write ‘Dear Associate Professor’ and ‘Dear Assistant Professor’ not ‘Dear Doctor’ or ‘Dear Professor’.
rules.violation_condition: addressing an associate or assistant professor as 'Dear Doctor' or 'Dear Professor' in Australian correspondence
when: applies to Australian correspondence addressing associate or assistant professors
rules.why: G-4: specific address convention for associate/assistant professors.

examples.note: Written in full when surname omitted

parts.quote: Dear Doctor

examples.note: Abbreviated when surname is present

parts.quote: Dear Dr Muecke

rules.quote: When writing ‘Dear’ without the person’s name in emails and letters, write the title ‘Doctor’ in full.

when: applies when writing 'Dear' followed by the title without a person's surname
rules.why: G-4: specific rule for addressing doctor without surname.

covers.quote: Instead, address the person by ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’. Write the post-nominals for the knighthood after the name, followed by any other post-nominals. Don’t insert commas before or between the post-nominals.

examples.note: Dame rather than Doctor for knighted doctorate holder

rules.quote: If the holder of a doctorate is knighted, don’t address them as ‘Doctor’.

parts.quote: The research fellow Lydia Mbegngue wrote extensively on this topic.

examples.note: Plural title in lower case

parts.quote: Several postdoctoral fellows in the research facility met last week.

examples.note: Common noun in lower case

parts.quote: A provost oversees a university’s academic performance.

examples.note: Title before name modified by 'former' in lower case

parts.quote: They met with former medical director Tom Perera.

tags.specification: Generic titles include plural titles, common nouns, descriptive titles following a name, or titles before a name preceded by 'the' or modifiers like 'former'.
tags.violation_condition: capitalising a generic title, such as a plural title, common noun, title describing an individual, or title modified by 'the' or an adjective

rules.why: G-1 and G-2: heading and definition of generic titles consolidated.

anchor.quote: The first time you mention someone in body text, use their academic or professional title before their first name and last name, followed by post-nominals.

covers.quote: Use title, name and post-nominals at first mention
If you mention the individual again, only use the title and last name. Some academic titles have an accepted abbreviated title you can use after the first mention.

examples.note: First mention with title and full name; subsequent mention with abbreviated title and surname

parts.quote: Emeritus Professor Stephen Duckett has extensive experience in health care at senior leadership level. Professor Duckett’s membership of the RMIT Council concludes in 2022.

tags.violation_condition: mentioning an academic or professional in body text for the first time without their title before their first and last name, or failing to switch to title and last name only on subsequent mentions

when: on subsequent mentions, only use the title and last name (or accepted abbreviated title and last name)
rules.why: G-1 and G-2: first mention format and subsequent mention format are two sides of the mention rule.

anchor.quote: Don’t use commas before or between post-nominals.

covers.quote: Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles

examples.note: No commas between post-nominals

parts.quote: Professor Sally Wheeler OBE MRIA FAcSS FAAL

tags.violation_condition: a comma placed immediately before or between post-nominals

rules.why: G-4: explicit negative constraint on punctuation around post-nominals.

anchor.quote: If you mention the name again, use the title and last name, but don’t include the post-nominal.

covers.quote: Use post-nominals at first mention only
The first time you write a name in body text, use the academic and professional title along with the first and last name. Include the post-nominal for a civil or military honour in the title.

examples.note: First mention has post-nominal AO; second mention omits it

parts.quote: Dr Ziggy Switkowski AO has been chancellor of RMIT since 2011. Dr Switkowski is also chair of NBN Co.

tags.violation_condition: including a post-nominal when naming an individual on a second or subsequent mention in body text

when: applies in body text
rules.why: G-4: specific rule requiring omission of post-nominals on repeat mention.

anchor.quote: Retain any post-nominals for civil and military honours when using the shortened forms of titles.

covers.quote: Include post-nominals in the shortened forms of titles

examples.note: Post-nominals retained with shortened title and initials

parts.quote: Attendees: Dr Z Switkowski AO, Prof M Bean CBE, Dr S Andrews, Ms J Latchford, Prof S Duckett, Ms T McLaughin and Mr D Hoogstra.

tags.violation_condition: omitting civil and military honours post-nominals when using shortened forms of titles

rules.why: G-4: heading restated by single sentence rule.

anchor.quote: Don’t include both ‘Dr’ (doctorate) and ‘PhD’ (Doctor of Philosophy) for the one name.
anchor.suffix: It is conventional to use eithe

examples.note: Either Dr or PhD, never both together

parts.quote: Dr Zdenka Svoboda or Zdenka Svoboda PhD

tags.specification: Use either the title 'Dr' or the post-nominal 'PhD' / 'LLD', but not both.
tags.violation_condition: using both 'Dr' and 'PhD' (or a PhD equivalent like 'LLD') for the same person's name

when: does not apply to medical practitioners who hold a doctorate (e.g. 'Dr ... MD PhD')
rules.why: G-4: distinct negative constraint on combining Dr and PhD.

anchor.quote: Don’t include post-nominals for master and bachelor degrees in correspondence.

tags.violation_condition: including bachelor or master degree post-nominals in correspondence

when: applies in correspondence (emails and letters)
rules.why: G-4: explicit negative constraint on degree post-nominals in correspondence.

anchor.quote: Use ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’ after the academic title.

examples.note: Dame after Chancellor

parts.quote: Chancellor Dame Leonie Kramer AC DBE

examples.note: Sir after Chancellor

parts.quote: Chancellor Sir Albert Axon KBE

tags.specification: For an academic who is knighted, place 'Sir' or 'Dame' directly after the academic title.
tags.violation_condition: placing 'Sir' or 'Dame' before an academic title (e.g. Sir Professor instead of Professor Sir)

when: applies when an academic has been knighted
rules.why: G-4: specific order rule for academic titles combined with knighthoods.

anchor.quote: Don’t include a comma after these phrases.

covers.quote: Don’t include a comma after these phrases.

examples.note: No commas after opening or closing

parts.quote: Dear Associate Professor … Yours faithfully

examples.note: Incorrect commas after salutation and valediction

parts.quote: Dear Associate Professor, … Yours faithfully,

tags.specification: Australian Government style writes salutations and valedictions without trailing commas.
tags.violation_condition: a comma placed after a correspondence salutation or valediction (e.g. 'Dear Chancellor,', 'Yours sincerely,')

when: applies to opening salutations and closing valedictions in correspondence
rules.why: G-4: unified punctuation prohibition for correspondence salutations/valedictions across sections.

anchor.quote: For Australian correspondence, write ‘Dear Associate Professor’ and ‘Dear Assistant Professor’ not ‘Dear Doctor’ or ‘Dear Professor’.

tags.violation_condition: addressing an associate or assistant professor as 'Dear Doctor' or 'Dear Professor' in Australian correspondence

when: applies to Australian correspondence addressing associate or assistant professors
rules.why: G-4: specific address convention for associate/assistant professors.

anchor.quote: When writing ‘Dear’ without the person’s name in emails and letters, write the title ‘Doctor’ in full.

examples.note: Written in full when surname omitted

parts.quote: Dear Doctor

examples.note: Abbreviated when surname is present

parts.quote: Dear Dr Muecke

tags.violation_condition: writing 'Dear Dr' without a surname instead of 'Dear Doctor'

when: applies when writing 'Dear' followed by the title without a person's surname
rules.why: G-4: specific rule for addressing doctor without surname.

anchor.quote: If the holder of a doctorate is knighted, don’t address them as ‘Doctor’.

covers.quote: Instead, address the person by ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’. Write the post-nominals for the knighthood after the name, followed by any other post-nominals. Don’t insert commas before or between the post-nominals.

examples.note: Dame rather than Doctor for knighted doctorate holder

parts.quote: Dame Bridget Ogilvie AC DBE FRS FAA

tags.specification: Address the person by 'Sir' or 'Dame', followed by post-nominals for knighthood then other post-nominals, without commas.
tags.violation_condition: addressing a knighted doctorate holder as 'Doctor' instead of 'Sir' or 'Dame'

when: applies when a doctorate holder has been knighted
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidates rule on knighted holders of doctorates.
